claims.text: High-throughput computational screening can identify promising Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti high-entropy-alloy compositions.
The relevant composition window is Al below 25 at.% and Mn above 15 at.%.
Promising alloys can be processed by repeated arc-melting, drop-casting, homogenization at 1200 °C, and annealing at 700 °C.
The samples are prepared from elements of 99.9 wt% purity.
Mechanical testing is performed from room temperature to 700 °C.
Combining computational screening with controlled thermal processing enhances phase stability.
Combining computational screening with controlled thermal processing produces a finer microstructure through precipitation or ordering.
The screened Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti alloys have higher elevated-temperature yield strength than traditional ferritic superalloys.
The resulting microstructure contains nanoscale L21 precipitates within a BCC matrix.
The resulting microstructure may instead contain ordered L21 antiphase domains within a BCC matrix.
Computational screening directs alloy selection toward compositions favoring L21-phase stability.
Deviations from ideal stoichiometry promote nanoscale L21 precipitate formation during thermal processing.
Near-stoichiometric compositions favor formation of L21 antiphase domains.
L21 precipitates enhance yield strength through load-transfer strengthening.
Ordered L21 antiphase domains enhance yield strength through ordering strengthening.
Traditional alloys without high-throughput optimization generally have less-refined microstructures.
Traditional alloys have lower elevated-temperature yield strengths than the optimized alloys.
The approach is effective only where the high-throughput predictions are valid, stated as Al below 25 at.% and Mn above 15 at.%.
Compositions outside the stated window may undergo different microstructural evolution.
The quantitative property improvement and balance between precipitates and antiphase domains depend on exact composition, annealing duration, and processing parameters.

contradictions.description: The design says optimized and outside-window controls receive the same processing, whereas the falsification rule compares optimized samples with controls processed by conventional methods.
The baseline is defined as having less-controlled thermal processing, but the proposed controls are subjected to the same controlled thermal-processing sequence as the optimized samples.
